title: Treasury Laws Amendment (OECD Multilateral Instrument) Bill 2018
short_title: Treasury Laws Amendment (OECD Multilateral Instrument) Bill 2018

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would give an international tax convention legal force in Australia, enabling changes to bilateral tax treaties addressing avoidance and resolving cross-border tax disputes.
It would modify agreements nominated by Australia and the relevant treaty partner after ratification, with the changes depending on their respective choices and reservations.
Different commencement rules would govern withholding taxes, other taxes and dispute procedures, so the convention's practical effect would vary between treaties and tax categories.
changes: Covered treaties could deny benefits where obtaining them was a principal purpose and granting them conflicted with the treaty's object and purpose.
Taxpayers could present eligible treaty disputes to either jurisdiction's competent authority where the relevant convention provision applied.
Eligible unresolved disputes could proceed to binding arbitration where the arbitration provisions were adopted, subject to reservations limiting the cases covered.
summary.affected: Taxpayers using covered bilateral tax agreements and the tax authorities responsible for those agreements would be affected.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Leigh
speeches.brief: The Labor member moved a second reading amendment noting the Coalition's failure to close multinational tax loopholes and improve tax haven transparency, while supporting the bill to implement the OECD multilateral convention. Labor also criticised the government for claiming credit for tax measures it had previously opposed and outlined its own plan to tighten tax transparency, close loopholes, and crack down on tax havens.

speeches.speaker: Matt Keogh
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the Turnbull government has failed to curb multinational tax avoidance, noting one in five of Australia's biggest companies paid no tax in three years and that Goldman Sachs paid zero tax on $1.8 billion revenue, while the government rejected key anti-avoidance articles 10 and 12 of the OECD multilateral instrument. They proposed Labor's alternative policies, including public country-by-country reporting, closing debt deduction loopholes (adding $5.4 billion over a decade), introducing a beneficial ownership registry, and rewarding whistleblowers.

speeches.speaker: Matt Thistlethwaite
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the amendment to the Treasury Laws Amendment Bill, noting the government declined to adopt articles 10 and 12 of the OECD convention targeting tax havens. A future Shorten Labor government would review that decision and, if elected, require large extractive companies to disclose payments on a country-by-country and project-by-project basis from 2020.

speeches.speaker: Kelly O'Dwyer
speeches.brief: The government argued its anti-avoidance laws have raised $7 billion in tax liabilities and collected $4.1 billion, including $1 billion from ecommerce companies, while Labor opposed these measures. The bill will modify 31 of Australia's 44 bilateral tax treaties to align with international best practice on curbing multinational tax avoidance.
